title: The LLM wrote "blood sprays" while the dice said MISS. Here's the turn-order change that fixed it, and the bug that finally forced it.
author: Merowingus
selftext:
I'm the solo dev of Divergentum, a commercial solo D&D 5e game with an LLM dungeon master. This post is about one engineering problem, not about the game, so here is exactly where AI is used up front:

* **Narration:** Gemini 2.5 Flash writes the story text and picks tags that say what the player did.
* **Everything with consequences** (dice, HP, damage, inventory, spell slots, loot) is deterministic server code following SRD 5.1. No model output is ever trusted as a number.
* **Art:** backgrounds and portraits are a pre-generated library, not generated live.
* \[Optional line, keep only if you're comfortable saying it: most of the codebase was written with an AI coding assistant and reviewed by me.\]

# The complaint that lasted for months

Players kept saying some version of "the combat doesn't match the story". In the logs it looked like this, in a single turn:

>Your axe bites deep. Blood sprays across the anvil. `Your attack: d20=10+2=12 vs AC13: MISS`

It was never a random bug. It was the order of operations:

1. Player acts.
2. The model writes the scene, **blind**, because the roll doesn't exist yet.
3. The server rolls the d20 after the text is written.
4. The player sees prose and a roll line side by side.

A model asked to write a fight scene without knowing the result writes the dramatic version: the hero hits. The server then rolls honestly and misses about half the time. The disagreement wasn't an error rate, it was guaranteed by the pipeline.

[Image 1: turn order, before and after](https://preview.redd.it/p05g9tlivrrh1.png?width=1206&format=png&auto=webp&s=bfa386bf0e327b5fbbd59ce34ba18468d0ed9bee)



# Three fixes that treated the symptom

1. **"Describe the swing, not the result."** The model ignored it regularly. A deliberately neutral fight scene is a bad fight scene, and the model enhances for the better prose, not for the instruction.
2. **A safety net on narrated deaths.** If the text sounds like the enemy died while the server still shows HP, end the fight. This fixed the worst case (an enemy still hitting a player who just read that they won) but it meant **text now controlled mechanics**.
3. **A fallback spawn.** Sometimes the model narrated a fight without ever declaring an enemy, so nothing was rolled and the hero risked nothing. If the hero attacks and no enemy exists, the server invents one.

Fixes 2 and 3 met each other about a month later.

# The blacksmith who respawned every turn

A player reported that the enemy "appears and hits, then his health bar vanishes and only I hit". The log showed four consecutive turns with four different enemies (Thug AC11, Commoner AC10, Opponent AC13, Dangerous opponent AC14, "Round 1" fifteen turns into the fight), while the story was about one blacksmith the whole time.

The narrator had given the smith a stylistic tic: "dead eyes", "he looked like a corpse". That is a description of a living man. The safety net saw death words and closed the fight. The health bar vanished, the counter-attack (which lived in the branch that no longer ran) stopped, the player swung at nothing, and the fallback spawned a brand new enemy at full HP. Repeat whenever the narrator liked its own metaphor.

[Image 2: the respawn loop](https://preview.redd.it/d9w3ae5nvrrh1.png?width=1160&format=png&auto=webp&s=c82781c263f6cf0967346d899ecade41c11a5dcb)

# The actual fix: roll first

None of the three earlier fixes touched the cause. So we did what a human DM does: roll, look, then describe.

* The server rolls **before** the model is called and puts the results in the prompt as facts.
* One d20 per turn for the hero, shared by every attack option (weapon, beast form, each attack spell). Otherwise the model, choosing between axe and spell, would effectively be choosing its own best roll.
* The model narrates the known result and returns a tag naming which option it used. The server applies only that option. No tag, no hit, whatever the prose says.
* A number alone isn't enough (2 damage and 14 damage both read as "a terrible blow"), so the prompt also carries a weight word derived from damage as a share of the enemy's max HP: `glancing`, `modest`, `solid`, `crippling`, `devastating`. The same 4 damage is a scratch on a bear and near-fatal on a rat. The model is not allowed to write the number itself.

Then the old safety net had to lose its power. Once the server dictates exact damage and remaining HP, prose proves nothing about the fight. A fight now ends on HP = 0 or an explicit tag. The death detector stayed, but only as telemetry: it measures how well the model obeys the numbers it was given.

# What this does not solve

* Skill checks: the die is prepared, but binding it to the specific check is still the next step, so the model can still invent that number.
* Sneak attack dice are rolled late, because the right to use it only becomes known from the tag the model returns after writing.
* A rage turned on this turn starts paying next turn, since numbers are final before the text exists. That's a direct consequence of the architecture and I kept it.
* The fallback enemy still has a generic name ("Opponent") while the story names an NPC.

The broader lesson I took: in a game where a model writes the text, anything with consequences has to belong to the server, and **the order of operations beat every instruction I ever put in the prompt.** Twice I tried to negotiate with the model in words. Only removing the possibility of disagreement worked.

# Two questions

**For developers:** if you have an LLM narrating around real mechanics, do you roll before or after the model writes? My open problem is that I don't know in advance whether the player's action is a weapon or a spell (that arrives with the model's reply), so I pre-roll one d20 and derive a result per option. Is there a cleaner way, or do you avoid the problem by making the player choose the action type explicitly in the UI?

**For players:** does knowing the dice were rolled before the prose was written make a fight feel more real, or more mechanical? What would you want the narration to do when the roll is a near miss?

*Divergentum is on web and Android if you want to see it in practice (divergentum.com), but I'm posting for the discussion of the problem.*

comments.body: if I used AI I imagine I'd copy and paste this and say \`ai summarize then write a concise reply demonstrating my expertise and understanding\`

comments.author: BanjoThunderbird
comments.body:
I really hope no one engages with the actual content of this post or goes to their website. An internet forum is for discussion between humans, if we wanted to read what AI has to say we would just talk to Claude.

>\[Optional line, keep only if you're comfortable saying it: most of the codebase was written with an AI coding assistant and reviewed by me.\]

Like did you even read it?

replies.body: These type of posts need to be banned, it’s laughable
